title: Gravis UltraSound ports and GF1 registers
covers: The Gravis UltraSound's I/O ports at the card's base block, 2X0/2X6/2X9/2XB/2XF and 3X0-3X7 plus the mixer's 7X6 and the UltraMax codec's four ports, and the GF1's indexed registers: the voice registers 0x00-0x0E with the read aliases 0x80-0x8F, and the global registers 0x41-0x4C, as the Lowlevel ToolKit documents them and DOSBox-X handles them.

rows.text: A write of 2X0 sets the mix control byte: bits 0-2 enable line in, line out and mic in, and bit 3 powers the latches.
The same write sets bits 4-6: IRQ combining, MIDI loopback, and which latch set, IRQ or DMA, the next write to 2XB reaches.
The document warns that the latch supply must stay on once enabled, or the IRQ and DMA lines float and raise random IRQs.
A write also clears the control register select and marks the IRQ and DMA latches as reprogrammed.
The IRQ status register is at 2X6, not at 3X6.
A read of 2X6 gives the pending IRQ bits: 0 MIDI transmit, 1 MIDI receive, 2 timer 1, 3 timer 2, 5 wavetable, 6 volume ramp, 7 DMA terminal count.
A read also counts rapid polls under the clear-on-polling option and, after five hundred, clears the DMA terminal count bit so a stuck game continues.
A write sets the Sound Blaster reset flag and, with the capture bit on, notifies the Sound Blaster emulation.
2X8 maps to the same location as the AdLib board's control register.
Writing 4 to 2X8 selects the timers.
A read of 2X8 sets bit 6 when timer 1 has expired and bit 5 when timer 2 has.
The read also reports the captured writes in bits 0, 3 and 4, the timer IRQs in bits 1 and 2, and a timer expiry in bit 7.
While the Sound Blaster emulation poses as the AdLib, a read returns the status byte it left in the latch.
Once 4 is written to 2X8, 2X9 is timer control: bit 0 starts timer 1, bit 1 timer 2, bits 6-5 mask them, bit 7 clears the IRQ.
Bits 3-4 are reserved, bit 5 masks timer 2, bit 6 masks timer 1 and bit 7 clears the timer IRQ.
Without the tool kit in charge, the byte is captured as AdLib data for the Sound Blaster emulation instead of driving the timers.
A read clears the captured-write flag and returns the byte the Sound Blaster emulation left.
2XB is the IRQ control register while bit 6 of 2X0 is set and the DMA control register while it is clear.
The IRQ control register selects the GF1 IRQ in bits 2-0 and the MIDI IRQ in bits 5-3: 1 to 7 are IRQ 2, 5, 3, 7, 11, 12, 15.
Bit 6 combines both IRQs on channel 1's, and the note says the second selector must then be 0 or a bus conflict arises.
The DMA control register selects the first DMA channel in bits 2-0 and the second in bits 5-3, 1 to 5 choosing DMA 1, 3, 5, 6 or 7.
Bit 6 combines both channels on the first, and the document notes that sharing a DMA without it raises a bus conflict.
The document says the two latches must be written in the right order or unpredictable things may happen.
The IRQ and DMA selectors decode through two tables of eight entries: 0 none, then IRQ 2, 5, 3, 7, 11, 12, 15 and DMA 1, 3, 5, 6, 7.
The card accepts the write only on the I/O cycle right after 2X0 or 2XF armed the latches, and ignores it otherwise.
The write also records whether the two selectors name the same IRQ or DMA, for the conflict warning.
Register 0 is the pre-3.4 control register and registers 1-4 are unused.
With register 5 selected, a write of 0 clears the IRQs at power-up.
With register 6 selected, a write's bits 1 and 2 enable the MIDI and joystick port address decode.
With register 5 selected, the write only logs the value at src/hardware/gus.cpp:1726 and clears no IRQ.
With register 6 selected, the write only logs the value at src/hardware/gus.cpp:1722 and enables neither decode.
Bits 2-0 and 5-3 select the GF1 and MIDI IRQs as documented, but bit 7, which the document reserves, makes a captured Sound Blaster write raise an NMI instead.
2XF is valid only on boards of revision 3.4 and above, where a bank of six registers exists at 2XB.
A write of 2XF selects which of the six registers at 2XB is talked to.
A read of 2XF gives 02h on a MAX or ICS card and ffh otherwise.

A read of 2XA returns the AdLib command byte last written to 2X8.

rows.text: 2XC is the Sound Blaster DSP command port the emulation adds at the card's base.
A write of 2XC stores the byte in the latch and marks a captured Sound Blaster write.
A read of 2XC returns the byte last stored in that latch.

rows.text: 2XE is a Sound Blaster port the emulation keeps at the card's base.
A write of 2XE stores the byte in the latch it owns.
A read of 2XE returns the byte last stored there.
3X0 is write-only for the MIDI control byte and read-only for the MIDI status byte.
The control byte's bits 0 and 1 master-reset the interface when set, and toggling them will normally raise a transmit-buffer-empty IRQ.
Bits 5 and 6 together enable the transmit IRQ and bit 7 the receive IRQ.
The status byte reports receive full in bit 0, transmit empty in bit 1, framing and overrun errors in bits 4 and 5, and a pending interrupt in bit 7.
The MIDI interface behaves identically to a 6850 UART.
The status bits are set by the MIDI interrupt check and by the transmit completion.
3X1 holds the MIDI transmit and receive registers, each eight bits wide.
A write of 3X1 transmits the byte.
A read of 3X1 returns the received byte.
A write while the interface is held in reset is dropped.
The byte is delivered when the transmit event fires, and loops back into the receiver when loopback is on.
A read also clears the receive-full status bit and rechecks the MIDI IRQ.
3X2 is the page or voice select register: it chooses which voice's registers the next accesses reach, from 0 to the active voice count.
A write of 3X2 selects the voice.
A read returns the last value written to 3X2 or to the data ports on pre-InterWave cards.
3X3 is the GF1 and global register select, read and written.
A write of 3X3 selects the indexed register the data port reaches.
A read returns the last value written to 3X2-3X5, which need not be the index selected.
A write also clears the stored 16-bit data latch.
3X4 is the global data low byte: a 16-bit I/O there transfers a whole 16-bit register, and an 8-bit I/O only its low part.
A write of 3X4 stores the low byte, and a 16-bit write executes the register at once.
A read of 3X4 returns the selected register's value, executing the read.
3X5 is the global data high byte: an 8-bit transfer for an 8-bit register, or the high part of a 16-bit one.
A write of 3X5 stores the high byte and executes the register.
A read of 3X5 returns the high byte of the selected register.
3X6 is the ICS-2101 mixer data port, or on a MAX the write-only UltraMax control register, and the software must know which device is there.
The UltraMax control register's bits 0-3 choose the X of the codec's base 3XC, bits 4 and 5 the capture and playback DMA width, and bit 6 enables the codec.
On a card with the ICS mixer the byte goes to the mixer's data port instead.
On a MAX a read of 3X6 gives the revision id byte.
3X7 reads or writes the DRAM byte at the address that registers 43 and 44 point at.
A write of 3X7 stores the byte into DRAM at that address.
A read of 3X7 returns the DRAM byte at that address.
7X6 reads the board revision on cards of 3.7 or later.
ff means no ICS mixer, 5 a 3.7 with flip problems, 6-9 a 3.7 or later with the mixer, and 0Ah and up an UltraMax.
A read of 7X6 gives that revision byte.
7X6 is the ICS-2101 mixer's control port, whose registers Chapter 5 describes.
A write of 7X6 sets the mixer's register address.
The codec answers at 3XC-3XF as four ports: address select, data, status and PIO, one address each.
On a daughter card the codec sits at 530, 604, E80 or F40 instead, and its register map is the CS4231's own datasheet.
The four codec ports are all read and written.
A read gives ff while the codec is disabled and the codec's own port value once it is enabled.
The four codec ports are installed at the base the UltraMax control register selects.
A write is dropped while the codec is disabled, and a new sample rate retunes the mixer channel.
Register 0 is the 8-bit Voice Control register of a voice.
Bit 0 reports the voice stopped, bit 1 stops it, bit 2 chooses 16-bit data, bit 3 loops and bit 4 loops bidirectionally.
Bit 5 enables the wavetable IRQ, bit 6 sets the direction and bit 7 reports an IRQ pending.
Bits 0, 6 and 7 are self-modifying: the GF1 sets them when the voice stops, changes direction or holds an IRQ.
Register 0x80 reads the voice control register back.
Register 1 is the 16-bit Frequency Control register.
Bits 15-10 are the integer part and bits 9-1 the fraction; bit 0 is not used.
The amount added to (or subtracted from) the current position gives the next: less than 0 it interpolates, greater than 1 it skips data bytes.
Register 0x81 is the read counterpart of the frequency control register.
Register 2 is the high part of the voice's start address.
Its bits 12-0 are address lines 19-7 of the start; bits 15-13 are not used.
Register 0x82 is the read counterpart of the start address high register.
Register 3 is the low part of the voice's start address.
Bits 15-9 are address lines 6-0 and bits 8-5 the fractional start address; bits 4-0 are not used.
Register 0x83 is the read counterpart of the start address low register.
Register 4 is the high part of the voice's end address.
Its bits 12-0 are address lines 19-7 of the end; bits 15-13 are not used.
Register 0x84 is the read counterpart of the end address high register.
Register 5 is the low part of the voice's end address.
Bits 15-9 are address lines 6-0 and bits 8-5 the fractional end address; bits 4-0 are not used.
Register 0x85 is the read counterpart of the end address low register.
Register 6 is the volume ramp rate.
Bits 5-0 are the step added each time, from 1 to 63, and bits 7-6 define how often it is applied.
Register 7 is the starting volume of a ramp.
Bits 7-4 are the exponent and bits 3-0 the mantissa of that starting volume.
Register 8 is the Volume Ramp End register.
Bits 7-4 are the exponent and bits 3-0 the mantissa; the register sets the ending position of a volume ramp.
The document asks for a starting volume below the ending one, turning on the decreasing bit to ramp down.
Register 9 is the Current Volume register.
Bits 15-12 are the exponent and bits 11-4 the mantissa, stored as the current volume; bits 3-0 are reserved and set to zero.
The register carries four extra bits of precision that a volume ramp uses.
The GF1 updates this register itself while it ramps.
The document asks the register to be set to the volume the ramp begins at.
Register 0x89 is the read counterpart of the current volume register.
Register 0xA is the Current Location HIGH register.
Bits 12-0 are the high 13 address bits, lines 19-7, stored into the current address; bits 15-13 are reserved and set to zero.
Register 0x8A is the read counterpart of the current location HIGH register.
Register 0xB is the Current Location LOW register.
Bits 15-9 are the low seven address bits, lines 6-0, and bits 8-0 a nine-bit fractional position, stored into the current address.
Register 0x8B is the read counterpart of the current location LOW register.
Register 0xC is the Pan Position register.
Bits 3-0 are stored as the pan position, 0 full left and 15 full right; bits 8-4 are reserved.
Register 0x8C is the read counterpart of the pan position register.
Register 0xD is the Volume Ramp Control register.
Bit 0 reports the ramp stopped, bit 1 stops it by hand and bit 2 raises an IRQ at the rollover without stopping; bits 0-2 are stored.
Bit 3 loops from end to start, bit 4 loops both ways and bit 5 enables the IRQ at the end of the ramp; bits 3-5 are stored.
Bit 6 is stored as the ramp direction, 0 increasing and 1 decreasing.
Register 0x8D is the read counterpart of the ramp control register, and its bit 7 reports a pending ramp IRQ.
The document points the reader to its section on hardware volume ramping.
DOSBox-X raises the voice's ramp IRQ when bits 7 and 5 of the written byte are both set, and clears it otherwise.
Register 0xE is the Active Voices register.
Bits 7-6 must be set to one and bits 5-0 hold the number of voices less one.
The document gives a range of 14 to 32 voices and forces any smaller value up to 14.
DOSBox-X takes bits 4-0 of the byte as the count less one.
A write of 0xE also copies the byte into the register-select index.
DOSBox-X raises a count below three by two on a Classic or MAX, and only a Interwave is forced up to fourteen.
With ignore channel count while active set, DOSBox-X refuses a write to 0xE while the DAC is enabled and logs it.
Writing 0xE also recomputes the active mask, the base frequency and each voice's ramp and sample rate.
Register 0x41 is the DRAM DMA Control register.
Bit 0 starts the DMA transfer and bit 1 is stored as its direction, 1 taking data out of the card.
Bits 2-4 are stored: bit 2 picks an 8- or 16-bit DMA channel and bits 3-4 divide the DMA rate by one to four.
Bits 5-7 are stored: bit 5 enables the terminal count interrupt, bit 6 is the data size and bit 7 inverts the high bit.
A read of 0x41 returns bit 6 set while the terminal count IRQ is pending.
Reading 0x41 also acknowledges and clears the pending terminal count IRQ.
A read of 0x41 starts a DMA transfer when dma_enable_on_dma_control_polling is set and the channel is unmasked, DMA is off and no terminal count is pending.
Register 0x42 is the DMA Start Address register.
Bits 15-0 are address lines 19-4, so a transfer starts on a 16-byte boundary, or 32-byte on a 16-bit channel.
DOSBox-X also returns the DMA start address on a read of 0x42.
A card reset and a DMA event transfer also rewrite the DMA start address.
Registers 0x43 and 0x44 are the DRAM I/O address registers.
Register 0x43 is the lower 16 address lines and register 0x44 the upper four.
The address picks the DRAM byte that port 3X7 reads or writes.
Register 0x45 is the Timer Control register.
The byte is stored as the timer control: bit 2 enables timer 1's IRQ and bit 3 timer 2's, the other bits reserved and set to zero.
A read of 0x45 returns the timer control byte last written.
DOSBox-X stores the byte, sets the timers' IRQ enables from bits 2 and 3, but uses reserved bits 5 and 1 for the 2X6 capture and AdLib data capture.
Registers 0x46 and 0x47 are the Timer 1 and Timer 2 counts.
The counts are loaded, count up to 0xFF and generate an IRQ; timer 1 ticks every 80 microseconds, timer 2 every 320.
DOSBox-X ticks timer 1 every 80 microseconds and timer 2 every 320, timing each from the written value up to 0x100, one count past the document's 0xFF.
Register 0x49 is the Sampling Control register.
Bit 0 starts sampling, bit 1 picks stereo over mono and bit 2 the 8- or 16-bit DMA width.
Bits 3-4 are reserved and set to zero, bit 5 enables the terminal count IRQ and bit 7 inverts the high bit; these bits are stored.
A read of 0x49 returns bit 6 set while the DMA terminal count IRQ is pending.
Reading 0x49 returns the DMA control byte with its terminal count bit, not the sampling byte.
DOSBox-X stores the sampling byte but starts or stops the transfer from bit 0 of the DMA control byte, not from these bits.
DOSBox-X stores bit 5 and bit 7 of the sampling byte and acts on the DMA control byte instead.
Register 0x4C is the reset register.
Bit 0 holds the GF1 in reset while zero and runs it while one.
Bit 1 enables the DAC output and bit 2 the GF1's master IRQ.
The register normally holds 0x07 while the application runs.
Reading 0x4C returns the reset byte, its bit 2 taken from the IRQ enable.
With globalread80alias on, DOSBox-X clears bit 7 of an index above 0x8F, so a read of 0xCC reaches 0x4C.
A reset also sets the AdLib command register to 85, clears the AdLib status and clears the DRAM peek and poke address.

rows.text: Register 0x10 is the undocumented register DOSBox-X names for Fast Tracker 2.
DOSBox-X accepts a write to register 0x10 and does nothing with it.
Register 0x8E is the Active Voices register.
The Active Voices value is voice independent.
DOSBox-X returns bits 7-5 set and, in bits 4-0, the channel count the program wrote less one.
A reset sets the count to 14, so a read of 0x8E after a reset returns 0xED.
Register 0x8F is the IRQ Source register, listed as IRQ Status (Voice independent).
Bits 0-4 hold the number, 0-31, of the interrupting voice and bit 5 is always 1; bits 6 and 7 read 0 for a volume ramp or wavetable IRQ.
The IRQ Source register is global and read-only: one copy serves all voices.
A read clears the associated IRQ bits of the interrupting voice.
Voices interrupting at once make the register read like a FIFO, each read reporting the next pending voice.
The handler is asked to keep reading until a read has both IRQ bits set, which leaves no voice IRQ to service.
The handler is asked to ignore a further IRQ from the same voice and reason until the voice stops, its IRQ enable is off or its end moves.
DOSBox-X also clears bits 5 and 6 of the IRQ status register 2X6 when 0x8F is read.
